item.title: SpaceX Aims for Starship Launch on Friday. Here’s What to Know.
item.description: The audacious maneuver planned for Friday is a key step toward the company’s goal of making rockets fully reusable.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:description: The Super Heavy booster for Starship preparing for launch ahead of Flight 15 at SpaceX’s Starbase in Texas on Wednesday.

item.title: These Male Dolphins Do Something Rare: Day Care
item.description: Male Franciscana dolphins are exceptional babysitters. Scientists are trying to figure out if they are thoughtful fathers or just hope to be.
item.dc:creator: Fanni Daniella Szakál

item.title: These Killer Female Apes Challenge the ‘Man the Hunter’ Origin Story
item.description: Bonobos are as closely related to humans as chimps. New evidence that female bonobos are the primary hunters could radically alter our understanding of early human societies.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Mitchell Brown

item.title: 25 Years After the Anthrax Attacks, America Remains Vulnerable
item.description: Letters filled with anthrax spores exposed flaws in the United States’ biosecurity systems. Experts say many of those issues still exist.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway

item.title: Could Alien Life Thrive in Sulfuric Acid Instead of Water?
item.description: Best known for dissolving bodies in bathtubs, sulfuric acid has the potential to be the elixir of life on other worlds.
item.dc:creator: Natalie Wolchover

item.title: El Niño Is Hitting California Hard
item.description: Rising sea levels and violent weather are testing residents in some of the most picturesque cities along the Pacific Coast.
item.dc:creator: David Gelles and Gabriela Bhaskar

item.title: How Did Greek Fire Work? And 6 Other Lost Inventions.
item.description: Even once-widespread innovations have been forgotten, leaving scholars puzzling over the details.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway, William J. Broad and Franz Lidz

item.title: An Anti-Trump Protest. Police Threats. Inside a Rift in Diabetes Research.
item.description: It began with a protest at an American Diabetes Association conference. Now a resulting boycott has caused a scientific slowdown, with no end in sight.
item.dc:creator: Eric Boodman
item.media:credit: Anna Liminowicz for The New York Times
item.media:description: Dr. Steven Kahn, director of the University of Washington’s diabetes research center, was stopped, along with other eminent scientists, from distributing leaflets at a major diabetes conference in New Orleans.

item.title: Malawi Lacks Money to Fund its El Niño Plans
item.description: The question is being asked across the developing world, where hunger risk is high from the extreme weather El Niño is expected to bring. Malawi has a big plan, but little money.
item.dc:creator: Chico Harlan, Golden Matonga and Joao Silva
item.media:description: Tilling a field in anticipation of the seasonal rains in Namasoko, a village in the Phalombe district in southern Malawi.

item.title: The Russian Scientist Behind the Deadly Novichok Nerve Agents Has Died
item.description: Vladimir Uglev, a lead developer of a Cold War-era chemical weapon used on the dissident Alexei Navalny, later turned against the government. He was 80.
item.dc:creator: Clay Risen

item.title: ‘Fight Harder,’ U.N. Chief António Guterres Implores, Rousing Climate Ambassadors at COP31
item.description: The United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, spoke at COP31, a meeting aimed at reducing emissions, amid a sharp drop in attendance by world leaders.
item.dc:creator: Chico Harlan and Lisa Friedman
item.category: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
item.media:description: “Fossil fuel interests keep making a killing while killing our planet,” António Guterres, the United Nations secretary general, said at COP31 on Wednesday.

item.title: The U.S. Has Lost Its Measles-Elimination Status, Data Suggests
item.description: An international panel of scientific experts will convene on Tuesday to evaluate the status, but genetic data already shows the virus is once again entrenched in the United States.
item.dc:creator: Apoorva Mandavilli
item.media:description: Genetic analyses traced at least three measles chains of transmission to Texas last year.

item.title: Iran War Unexpectedly Drove Down Carbon Emissions This Year
item.description: It’s the first drop in planet-warming pollution since the pandemic in 2020. But researchers cautioned that the decline could be short-lived.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
item.media:description: Researchers believe the dip may be only temporary — if the war with Iran ends and the Strait of Hormuz reopens, oil and gas demand could easily bounce back.

item.title: What Is Congress’s Plan to Speed Up Energy Permits?
item.description: The sprawling bill, which has divided Democrats, would overhaul major environmental laws to streamline the permitting process.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.media:credit: Heather Rousseau/The Roanoke Times, via Associated Press
item.media:description: The legislation would overhaul several landmark environmental laws to make it easier for the federal government to approve all sorts of projects, from gas pipelines to subway expansions.

item.title: With Hopes Low and Temperatures High, Climate Summit Opens in Turkey
item.description: War, artificial intelligence and the Trump era have overshadowed climate change. But officials from nearly every nation are meeting to confront global warming.

item.title: Did These Scientists Find Evidence of Blood in a Dinosaur Bone?
item.description: Mineralized “structures” discovered in the bone were the fossilized remains of red blood cells, according to a recent study. Other experts aren’t so sure.
item.dc:creator: Stella Raine Chu
item.category: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
item.media:description: Fossilized remains from a hind limb of the dinosaur Aratasaurus at the Museu de Paleontologia Plácido Cidade Nuvens in Brazil.

item.title: How an Intern and a Biologist Rescued an Orphaned Walrus in Alaska
item.description: An injured five-month-old walrus was found huddled next to carcasses in remote Alaska after it became separated from its mother. Its rescue took days and lots of patience.
item.dc:creator: Ishani Desai

item.title: Top Astrophysicist Leaves U.S. After Trump Policies Affect Her Work

item.title: NASA Is Selecting Future Astronauts. Here’s How to Apply.
item.description: The space agency is recruiting its next class of space travelers for missions to low-Earth orbit and the moon. Applications are due Dec. 3.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:description: The new recruits would most likely participate in the Artemis program, which flew its first crewed mission, a loop around the moon, in April.

item.title: Doctors Absorb the Stunning Failure of Two High-Profile Heart Drugs
item.description: By every measure, the drugs were no better than placebos, full data revealed on Saturday. Was it the fault of the design of the studies, or our very hypotheses about heart disease?
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata

item.title: Still on the President’s Agenda: Daylight Saving Time
item.description: Following an election-year rout for Republicans, Trump castigated lawmakers for not passing the Sunshine Protection Act. Some scientists have warned against the change.
item.dc:creator: Lynne Peeples
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross for The New York Times
item.media:description: If the president were to sign a bill making daylight saving time permanent, most clocks in the U.S. could suddenly spring forward, pushing sunrise to after 9 a.m. in many places for several weeks.

item.title: Biotech Firm Claims Some Credit for Groundbreaking Virus Research
item.description: Radical Numerics turned heads with its announcement about a novel treatment. Now a former partner, Tabula Bioscience, says it performed much of the research.
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer
item.media:credit: Ben Pennington/The Boston Globe, via Getty Images
item.media:description: George Church, a prominent geneticist at Harvard, resigned as an adviser to Radical Numerics over concerns that it had presented experimental results produced by another company as its own.

item.title: Lonnie Thompson Has Died. He Dodged Avalanches to Preserve Climate History.
item.description: His observations helped establish shriveling mountain glaciers as an unmistakable consequence of human-caused warming. He was 78.
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhong
